15.stem: In the SAMPLE history mnemonic, the letter "A" stands for:
15.why: SAMPLE: Signs/symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last oral intake, Events. Allergies matter before you assist with meds.

15.stem: The "M" in SAMPLE history refers to:
15.why: Ask what drugs they take daily, including inhalers, nitro, insulin, and blood thinners — it shapes your differential and safety.

15.stem: When taking SAMPLE history, "L" stands for:
15.why: Last oral intake helps with hypoglycemia, overdose timing, and hospital prep. It is not lung sounds or LOC.

15.stem: In OPQRST, the "O" stands for:
15.why: Onset asks when the problem started and whether it was sudden or gradual — critical for ACS, stroke, and PE clocks.

15.stem: In OPQRST assessment of pain or discomfort, "Q" stands for:
15.why: Quality is how they describe it (crushing, sharp, burning). That wording helps separate cardiac, pulmonary, and musculoskeletal causes.

15.stem: The "R" in OPQRST asks about:
15.why: Region/radiation maps where it hurts and where it travels — jaw, arm, or back radiation raises ACS concern.

15.stem: In OPQRST, "S" refers to:
15.why: Severity is the patient's numeric or descriptive intensity rating. Track it before and after treatment.

15.stem: The "T" in OPQRST stands for:
15.why: Timing covers constant vs intermittent, how long each episode lasts, and whether it is getting worse.

15.stem: On arrival at a medical call, scene size-up should FIRST include:
choices: Ensuring scene safety and determining the nature of illness
Starting an IV of normal saline
15.why: BSI/scene safety and NOI come before detailed history. You cannot treat if the scene is unsafe or the problem category is wrong.

15.stem: A patient with suspected meningococcal meningitis warrants which level of PPE emphasis?
choices: Gloves plus mask (and eye protection as indicated) due to droplet risk
No PPE if the patient denies fever
Full biohazard suit with positive-pressure respirator on every call
15.why: Meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets. Gloves plus surgical mask (and eye protection when splash risk exists) are standard EMT precautions.

15.stem: Standard precautions on a medical call mean you:
choices: Wear PPE only after confirming a positive culture
Skip gloves if the patient looks clean
Assume body fluids may be infectious and use appropriate barriers
Use N95 respirators for every minor complaint
15.why: Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious. Match PPE to the exposure risk, not to how healthy the patient looks.

15.stem: Which disease is MOST associated with airborne (not merely droplet) transmission precautions in EMS?
15.why: TB is the classic EMS airborne concern — N95/respirator and early notification. Most bacterial STIs and UTIs are not airborne.

15.stem: On the AVPU scale, a patient who opens eyes only when you shout their name is classified as:
15.why: Verbal (V) means they respond to voice but are not spontaneously alert. Pain requires a physical stimulus; U means no response.

15.stem: A patient who does not respond to voice but withdraws when you pinch the trapezius is:
15.why: Pain response without voice response = P on AVPU. That is still a life-threatening presentation needing airway vigilance.

15.stem: Which medical patient is the HIGHEST transport priority?
choices: Stable 40-year-old with a week of mild sinus congestion
Patient requesting a refill of allergy medication
Confused febrile patient with hypotension and mottled skin
Patient with a resolved nosebleed and normal vitals
15.why: Altered mentation plus fever and hypoperfusion scream sepsis/shock — lights-and-siren priority with hospital notification.

15.stem: Which cluster of findings BEST raises concern for sepsis in an adult?
choices: Isolated ankle sprain after a fall
Chronic stable hypertension with a normal exam
Fever or suspected infection with tachycardia, tachypnea, and altered mentation
15.why: Sepsis is infection plus a dysregulated host response. Fever/known source plus abnormal vitals and AMS = early hospital alert.

15.stem: Which of the following is a SIGN rather than a symptom?
choices: You observe diaphoresis and cool skin
The patient describes crushing chest pain
The patient says they feel dizzy
15.why: Signs are what you observe or measure. Symptoms are what the patient reports. Diaphoresis is a sign.

15.stem: Your general impression of a medical patient is formed primarily from:
choices: Overall appearance, work of breathing, and circulation as you approach
A complete neurologic exam before looking at ABCs
15.why: From the doorway: sick or not sick — appearance, breathing effort, and skin/perfusion cues guide urgency.

15.stem: For a responsive medical patient with no immediate life threat, after ABCs you typically:
choices: Perform a full trauma log-roll on every call
Obtain a focused history (OPQRST/SAMPLE) and focused exam
Wait until the ED to ask any questions
15.why: Stable responsive medical patients get a complaint-driven history and exam. Do not shotgun trauma maneuvers without indication.

15.stem: An unresponsive medical patient should be assessed with emphasis FIRST on:
choices: A complete allergy list from the fridge
Having the patient sign a refusal form
Airway, breathing, and circulation with rapid exam for life threats
15.why: Unresponsive = treat like a high-priority patient. Secure ABCs, check glucose early, and gather history from bystanders as able.

15.stem: "Index of suspicion" on a medical call means:
choices: Your awareness of how serious the patient's condition might be based on clues
A formal legal diagnosis you must write on the PCR
15.why: Index of suspicion is your clinical antenna — NOI, appearance, and risk factors tell you how bad this could be.

15.stem: Tunnel vision during medical assessment is dangerous because you may:
choices: Fixate on one finding and miss a competing life threat
15.why: Example: chasing a drunk story and missing hypoglycemia or head injury. Stay systematic.

15.stem: A medical identification bracelet is MOST useful because it can:
choices: Replace the need for vital signs
Confirm the patient does not need transport
Reveal allergies, medical conditions, or implanted devices
15.why: MedicAlert tags often list diabetes, seizures, allergies, or anticoagulants when the patient cannot speak.

15.stem: A patient who correctly states name, place, and approximate time is described as:
15.why: Orientation x3 is a quick mental-status screen. Loss of orientation is an early "sick" clue.

15.stem: For a stable medical patient, vital signs are generally reassessed about every:
15.why: Stable patients: ~every 15 minutes. Unstable: ~every 5 minutes and after each intervention.

15.stem: A field impression is BEST described as:
choices: Your working sense of the patient's problem based on assessment findings
Only what dispatch typed into the CAD
15.why: EMTs form a field impression (e.g., "suspected CHF") to guide treatment and destination — not a definitive hospital diagnosis.

15.stem: Which statement about hepatitis B and EMS is MOST accurate?
choices: It cannot be transmitted by blood exposure
Airborne N95 use alone prevents all hepatitis B
Vaccination and standard precautions reduce occupational risk
Only elderly patients can carry hepatitis B
15.why: HBV is bloodborne. Vaccination plus gloves/eye protection after exposure risk is the EMT defense — not an N95 for every call.

15.stem: HIV transmission risk for EMS providers is BEST reduced by:
choices: Only treating patients who deny HIV
Standard precautions and careful sharps handling
15.why: HIV is blood/body-fluid borne. Barriers and needle safety matter; you cannot screen by appearance or denial.

15.stem: When interviewing an anxious medical patient, the BEST approach is to:
choices: Use a calm tone, ask open then focused questions, and listen
Stand over them and speak as fast as possible
Only speak to family and ignore the patient
Refuse to explain procedures to reduce anxiety
15.why: Rapport improves history quality. Calm, clear questions beat rapid-fire interrogation.

15.stem: If a medical patient is unresponsive, useful history is MOST often obtained from:
choices: Family, caregivers, or bystanders on scene
15.why: Bystanders may know last known well, meds, diabetes, seizures, or overdose clues — ask before they leave.

15.stem: Which finding alone MOST strongly supports high-priority transport on a medical call?
choices: A healed surgical scar from years ago
Difficulty breathing with inability to speak full sentences
A normal resting pulse and SpO2 of 99%
15.why: Severe respiratory distress is a classic priority criterion. Chronic scars and mild allergies are not.

15.stem: A patient found on the floor after "passing out" with unknown events should be treated as:
choices: Medical only — trauma exam is never needed
Potentially medical and trauma until assessment clarifies
15.why: Syncope can cause a fall and head injury. Keep a trauma index of suspicion until you prove otherwise.

15.stem: During a known influenza outbreak, EMS providers should:
choices: Use appropriate PPE and follow agency infection-control guidance
Ignore PPE because "everyone already has it"
15.why: Outbreaks raise exposure risk. PPE, hand hygiene, and local protocols protect you and subsequent patients.

15.stem: The secondary assessment on a medical patient is intended to:
choices: Gather detailed history and a focused or full physical exam after life threats are addressed
15.why: Primary finds life threats; secondary digs into OPQRST/SAMPLE and exam details once ABCs are handled.

15.stem: Cool, pale, diaphoretic skin in a medical patient MOST suggests:
choices: A normal finding in all adults
15.why: Skin is a window to perfusion. Cool/clammy/pale = sympathetic response to hypoxia, shock, or hypoglycemia until proven otherwise.

15.stem: When applying a pulse oximeter during medical assessment, remember that:
choices: SpO2 replaces the need to assess breathing effort
A reading of 100% proves the airway is patent forever
Poor perfusion, nail polish, or cold extremities can give false readings
15.why: SpO2 is helpful but imperfect. Treat the patient — work of breathing and mentation still rule.

15.stem: The "E" in SAMPLE history asks about:
choices: Events leading up to the illness
15.why: Events reconstruct what happened before EMS arrival — onset activity, exposures, and preceding symptoms.

15.stem: The "P" in SAMPLE refers to:
15.why: Past history (diabetes, COPD, heart failure, seizures) frames the NOI. Provocation is the P in OPQRST.

15.stem: A confused febrile patient with low blood pressure who wants to "just sleep it off" should:
choices: Be encouraged to refuse without further evaluation
Be left with family without documentation
Be considered high risk — altered patients often lack decision-making capacity
Be assumed safe if they can walk to the couch
15.why: Altered mentation and shock signs undermine informed refusal. Follow agency AMA/capacity policy and advocate for transport.

15.stem: Dispatch information on a medical call is BEST used to:
choices: Lock in a final diagnosis before arrival
Decide that PPE is never needed
Prepare mentally and with equipment, while remaining ready to find something different
15.why: CAD clues help you stage gear, but patients often present differently. Reassess NOI on arrival.

16.stem: Use of accessory muscles of breathing MOST indicates:
choices: Increased work of breathing and respiratory distress
That the patient has no lung disease
16.why: Neck, intercostal, and abdominal muscle use means the patient is fighting to move air — a distress flag.

16.stem: A patient sitting upright, leaning forward with hands on knees to breathe is demonstrating:
16.why: Tripoding braces the chest wall and maximizes accessory muscle use. Treat as significant respiratory distress.

16.stem: Cyanosis of the lips and nail beds MOST suggests:
16.why: Blue skin/mucosa from desaturated hemoglobin is a late but serious oxygenation clue — support airway and oxygen.

16.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes hypoxia from hypoxemia?
choices: They are identical terms with no difference
Hypoxia means high CO2 only; hypoxemia means fever
Hypoxemia only occurs in trauma; hypoxia only in medical patients
Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the blood; hypoxia is inadequate oxygen at the tissue level
16.why: Hypoxemia = low PaO2/SpO2 in blood. Hypoxia = cells not getting enough O2. You can have one without the other in special cases.

16.stem: For most acutely ill medical patients without COPD, a common SpO2 target range is approximately:
choices: Exactly 100% at all times with maximum oxygen
16.why: Aim roughly mid-90s and up unless protocol says otherwise. Blind 100% forever is not always the goal; treat the patient.

16.stem: In suspected carbon monoxide exposure, standard pulse oximetry may be unreliable because:
choices: CO always lowers SpO2 to zero instantly
Many pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin and may read falsely high
SpO2 is never used in EMS
16.why: CO poisoning can look "normal" on SpO2 while the patient is hypoxic. High-flow oxygen and specialty CO-oximetry/ED care matter.

16.stem: Suctioning of the airway is indicated when you hear or see:
choices: Quiet, clear breathing with a patent airway
Gurgling and visible secretions, blood, or vomit in the airway
A patient who is speaking full sentences clearly
16.why: Gurgling means fluid in the airway. Suction before positive-pressure ventilation so you do not push vomit into the lungs.

16.stem: Which finding is a conceptual contraindication to CPAP at the EMT level?
choices: Pulmonary edema with intact mentation and adequate blood pressure per protocol
SpO2 of 90% in a speaking CHF patient
Increased work of breathing with crackles
Unresponsive patient unable to follow commands or protect the airway
16.why: CPAP needs a cooperative patient who can protect their airway. Unresponsive, vomiting, or hypotensive patients are typical exclusions.

16.stem: When assisting a patient with a prescribed metered-dose inhaler (MDI), you should:
choices: Confirm the medication is theirs, not expired, and follow local protocol/medical direction
Give it to every chest-pain patient without orders
Administer it only after needle decompression
16.why: EMTs assist with the patient's prescribed bronchodilator under protocol — verify the drug, dose, and indications first.

16.stem: Asthma is BEST characterized as:
choices: Reversible lower-airway inflammation, bronchospasm, and mucus production
Infection of the pleural space with pus
A clot lodged in a pulmonary artery
16.why: Asthma is reactive airway disease. Triggers cause wheeze, dyspnea, and accessory muscle use; severe attacks can progress to failure.

16.stem: Chronic bronchitis as a COPD phenotype is classically associated with:
choices: A productive cough for months and chronic sputum production
Exclusive occurrence in nonsmokers under age 20
16.why: "Blue bloater" chronic bronchitis features chronic productive cough and hypoxia risk. Smoking is a major risk factor.

16.stem: Emphysema is MOST associated with:
choices: A foreign body stuck in the trachea only
Fluid overload from left heart failure exclusively
Destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil
16.why: Emphysema destroys alveoli ("pink puffer," barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing). Gas exchange surface shrinks.

16.stem: Pursed-lip breathing in a COPD patient helps primarily by:
choices: Creating gentle back-pressure that can stent airways open during exhalation
16.why: Pursed lips slow exhalation and keep small airways from collapsing — a compensatory trick you should allow.

16.stem: Left-sided heart failure commonly causes dyspnea because:
choices: The trachea spontaneously collapses in every patient
Fluid backs up into the pulmonary circulation and alveoli
It always creates a tension pneumothorax
It only affects the legs and never the lungs
16.why: Left pump failure raises pulmonary pressures — crackles, hypoxia, and respiratory distress follow.

16.stem: A sudden-onset dyspnea patient who recently took a long flight and has unilateral leg swelling MOST suggests:
16.why: Immobility + DVT clues + sudden SOB/chest pain/hypoxia = PE until proven otherwise. High-flow O2 and rapid transport.

16.stem: Pneumonia in adults often presents with:
choices: Only painless ankle swelling without respiratory findings
Always bilateral wheezes that vanish with coaching
Normal vitals and no cough by definition
Fever, productive cough, and localized crackles or diminished sounds
16.why: Infection fills alveoli — fever, cough (often productive), pleuritic pain, and focal lung findings are classic.

16.stem: A anxious patient with carpopedal spasm, tingling around the mouth, and rapid deep breathing MOST likely has:
choices: Hyperventilation syndrome (after you rule out serious causes)
Confirmed STEMI requiring fibrinolysis by the EMT
Massive hemothorax requiring needle decompression by the EMT
16.why: Hyperventilation blows off CO2 and can cause perioral tingling and hand spasms. Still exclude hypoxia, PE, and metabolic causes.

16.stem: Spontaneous pneumothorax is MOST classically seen in:
choices: Tall, thin young adults, sometimes with sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnea
16.why: Primary spontaneous pneumo loves tall thin young males (and smokers). Sudden unilateral pain/SOB — support O2; decompression is ALS.

16.stem: Crackles (rales) heard on auscultation MOST often suggest:
choices: A completely clear pleural space with no pathology
Fluid or atelectasis in the smaller airways/alveoli
Normal findings in all sleeping adults
16.why: Crackles are discontinuous sounds — think pulmonary edema, pneumonia, or fibrosis, not stridor.

16.stem: Low-pitched rattling sounds that often clear somewhat with coughing are called:
16.why: Rhonchi suggest mucus in larger airways. Cough may temporarily clear them; pneumonia/bronchitis are common contexts.

16.stem: Which patient MOST clearly shows inadequate breathing requiring assisted ventilations?
choices: Altered patient with shallow, slow respirations and cyanosis
Speaking full sentences with SpO2 98% on room air
Anxiety with normal mentation and good tidal volume
16.why: Failure of rate, depth, or mentation = bag them. Dyspnea alone with good volume is not automatic BVM.

16.stem: Snoring respirations in an unresponsive patient usually indicate:
choices: Partial upper-airway obstruction, often by the tongue
A need for immediate needle decompression
16.why: Tongue falls back when mentation drops. Open the airway (head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw-thrust as indicated).

16.stem: Status asthmaticus refers to:
choices: A mild wheeze that resolves with one puff at home
Any patient who owns an inhaler
A severe asthma attack that does not respond to usual therapy and risks respiratory failure
16.why: Prolonged, refractory asthma is a crash airway risk — ALS backup, oxygen, and rapid transport.

16.stem: A barrel-shaped chest in a long-time smoker is MOST consistent with:
choices: Isolated deep vein thrombosis without lung involvement
16.why: Air trapping expands the AP chest diameter. Expect pursed lips and chronic dyspnea.

16.stem: Nasal flaring in a pediatric respiratory patient indicates:
choices: Only ear infection without respiratory stress
16.why: Flaring, retractions, and grunting are pediatric distress signs — do not wait for adult-style complaints.

16.stem: A febrile child sitting forward, drooling, and speaking in a muffled voice raises concern for:
choices: Simple allergic rhinitis — force them flat
Epiglottitis — avoid agitating and do not inspect the throat aggressively
Foreign body that always needs blind finger sweeps
16.why: Epiglottitis is an airway emergency. Keep the child calm, give oxygen as tolerated, and avoid throat probes that trigger obstruction.

16.stem: Croup is typically associated with:
choices: Only pink frothy sputum in elderly CHF
Sudden PE after long travel in adults
A barking cough and stridor in a viral upper-airway illness of young children
Complete absence of any respiratory sound changes
16.why: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) = barky cough, hoarseness, stridor. Cool night air sometimes helps; still assess for failure.

16.stem: Whooping cough (pertussis) is characterized by:
choices: Only painless neck stiffness without cough
Always a silent chest from day one
Fits of coughing that may end with a "whoop" and post-tussive vomiting
16.why: Pertussis causes prolonged coughing paroxysms. PPE matters — it spreads by droplets.

16.stem: Aspiration pneumonia risk is HIGHEST in which patient?
choices: Elderly patient with impaired swallowing after a stroke who was found with emesis
Alert athlete after a short jog
Child with a mild cold and clear sensorium who is eating normally
16.why: Depressed mentation and poor airway protection let vomit/food enter the lungs — suction and position matter.

16.stem: Gas exchange between air and blood primarily occurs in the:
16.why: Alveoli are the thin-walled air sacs where O2 and CO2 diffuse. Disease there (edema, pneumonia, emphysema) wrecks oxygenation.

16.stem: Air entering the pleural space and collapsing the lung is called:
16.why: Pneumothorax = air in the pleural space. Tension physiology with shock is ALS territory; EMTs support ABCs and transport.

16.stem: A dyspneic patient with SpO2 88% on room air who is speaking in short phrases MOST appropriately needs:
choices: Immediate surgical cricothyrotomy by the EMT
Supplemental oxygen titrated to improve SpO2 and distress per protocol
16.why: Hypoxemia plus distress = oxygen. Device choice (NC, NRB, BVM, CPAP) follows severity and protocol.

16.stem: Intercostal retractions indicate:
choices: The chest wall is being pulled inward by high negative pressures from severe distress
That lungs are overexpanded with zero disease
16.why: Retractions mean high work of breathing. Common in kids and severe asthma/COPD/CHF.

16.stem: Tidal volume refers to:
choices: The patient's body weight in kilograms
The amount of air moved in one normal breath
The number of alveoli destroyed by smoking
16.why: Minute ventilation = rate x tidal volume. Shallow breaths (low TV) can fail even if the rate looks "normal."

16.stem: Cystic fibrosis patients often present to EMS with:
choices: Always normal sputum and clear lungs
Thick mucus, chronic respiratory infections, and dyspnea
Exclusive cardiac chest pain without lung involvement
16.why: CF produces thick secretions and recurrent lung infections. Support oxygenation and bring usual meds/history.

16.stem: Bronchiolitis is MOST common in:
choices: Infants and young children, often after a viral illness with wheezing and distress
16.why: RSV bronchiolitis hits small airways in babies — watch for hypoxia, poor feeding, and apnea risk.

16.stem: Seesaw breathing in an infant (abdomen rises while chest falls) suggests:
choices: Normal quiet sleep breathing in all ages
16.why: Paradoxical chest/abdomen motion is a pediatric failure sign — prepare to assist ventilations.

16.stem: A conscious dyspneic patient should generally be allowed to:
choices: Be forced fully supine against their will
Assume a position of comfort, often sitting upright
Be placed prone with no monitoring
Be hung in Trendelenburg for all respiratory complaints
16.why: Upright/sitting usually eases work of breathing. Forcing flat often worsens distress (unless trauma/spine rules apply).

16.stem: Which finding is MORE ominous than loud diffuse wheezes in asthma?
choices: Improving speech and falling respiratory rate toward normal with better air movement
Mild cough after exercise that resolves at rest
Fatigue, declining mental status, and decreasing air movement
16.why: Tiring out and quieting lungs mean air is barely moving. That is peri-arrest respiratory failure territory.

16.stem: A nonrebreather mask is MOST appropriate when:
choices: The patient is apneic and needs artificial ventilation
The patient has a complete foreign-body obstruction still in place
The patient needs high-concentration oxygen and is breathing adequately on their own
16.why: NRB delivers high FiO2 to spontaneously breathing patients. Apnea needs BVM; obstruction needs removal first.
